strengths: The composite priority construction is simple and interpretable. The tier-based argument gives a clean expected per-key BST depth bound for arbitrary weight distributions, modulo an additive constant.
The paper pursues a useful unified objective: static optimality, external-memory B-trees, dynamic locality, and graceful degradation under prediction error.
The counterexamples for purely frequency-ordered priorities and coarser priority tiers clearly motivate why randomization and the proposed double-logarithmic bucketing are useful.
The entropy, cross-entropy, and log-score-error viewpoints provide natural ways to express prediction-dependent guarantees.
The experiments include several classical and learning-augmented baselines, multiple synthetic distributions, imperfect predictions, and repeated trials.
weaknesses: A central update guarantee appears false. Corollary 2.7 and Theorem C.2 claim O(|log(w'/w)|) rotations or touched nodes. Because the priority uses a floor, weights with w'/w arbitrarily close to one can cross a tier boundary, change priority by one, and cause a nonzero expected number of rotations. Moreover, the B-tree proof says the bound follows by deleting and reinserting the item, which only yields a bound depending on log(1/w)+log(1/w'), not their difference. The dynamic and robustness analyses rely on this unsupported guarantee.

The B-tree extension is not convincingly established. The proof applies the Golovin result separately to tier components while assuming B=O(C_t^(1/2)), although the actual tier population C_t can be arbitrarily small. It then combines independently maintained B-treaps without proving B-tree degree, occupancy, ordering, or update invariants. The simultaneous high-probability guarantee is also asserted without the necessary union-bound or small-component analysis.

The working-set result has an unresolved operation-order issue. At lookup i, the tree naturally contains the score from before accessing x(i), whereas the stated depth bound uses work(i,x(i)), which is defined using the interval until the next access. Updating first would require already locating the item or assuming an unmodeled direct pointer. The standard current working-set quantity corresponds to work(i-1,x(i)); a reindexing may salvage a total bound, but the stated per-access theorem and algorithm are not justified.

The robustness claims overstate what is proved. Theorem 2.13 supplies only an asymptotic upper bound through cross-entropy, not that the actual additional cost is exactly m times the KL divergence. Likewise, Theorems D.2 and D.11 infer cost(predicted)=cost(true)+O(error) from separate big-O upper bounds; this does not establish an additive comparison between the actual costs without a coupling or lower-bound argument.

Several static statements omit the unavoidable additive one. Since depth is defined as the number of vertices on the root-to-item path, O(log(1/w_x)) is false when w_x approaches one, and m times entropy alone can be below the mandatory m lookup cost. The correct forms require O(1+log(1/w_x)) and approximately m+mH(p). This affects the claimed identification with the static optimum.

The originality discussion is incomplete. The paper does not carefully compare its construction with classical biased or weighted randomized search trees and weighted treap variants that already target expected O(log(W/w_x)) access bounds. Consequently, the novelty of the principal static result is not adequately established.

The empirical evidence covers only static synthetic workloads. There are no experiments for the dynamic, working-set, B-tree, update-cost, or external-memory claims. The inaccurate-oracle generation procedure is insufficiently specified, error bars are undefined, no implementation is provided, and changing costs for non-learning baselines across KL levels suggest that prediction error may be confounded with changes in the underlying workload.

Numerous inconsistencies hinder verification: Figure 7's caption reverses properties used in its proof, Theorem 4.4 alternates between logarithm bases, the initialization uses tied priorities and violates earlier assumptions, Corollary C.5 cites itself, and several equations contain indexing or notation errors. These are especially concerning because they occur in already abbreviated proofs of the main extensions.

import random, statistics

def parent_depth(pr, x):
    # Cartesian max tree via stack, return depth node x 0-based
    n=len(pr); left=[-1]*n; right=[-1]*n; par=[-1]*n; st=[]
    for i,v in enumerate(pr):
        last=-1
        while st and pr[st[-1]]<v:
            last=st.pop()
        if st:
            right[st[-1]]=i; par[i]=st[-1]
        if last>=0:
            left[i]=last; par[last]=i
        st.append(i)
    d=0; y=x
    while par[y]>=0:d+=1;y=par[y]
    return d
for n in [10,100,1000,10000]:
    x=n//2; ds=[]
    for _ in range(20000 if n<1000 else 3000):
        pr=[random.random() for _ in range(n)]
        d0=parent_depth(pr,x)
        pr[x]=-1+random.random()*0.9 # below peers U(0,1)
        d1=parent_depth(pr,x)
        ds.append(d1-d0)
    print(n, statistics.mean(ds), max(ds), statistics.quantiles(ds,n=10)[8])

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-bnn74d2k/call-01adc1656aec4250883274e8b0b6b69b/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} contains an elegant central idea: discretizing log-log weights into priority tiers while randomly ordering keys within each tier yields a simple Treap construction for general, non-Zipfian weights.

The tier-counting and ancestor arguments behind the static BST result are concise and intuitive, and the counterexamples to simpler priority assignments help motivate the particular composite priority.
The paper ambitiously connects static optimality, prediction-error analysis, dynamic locality, and external-memory B-Trees within one framework.
The evaluation includes several classical and learning-augmented baselines, multiple synthetic distributions, inaccurate predictions, and repeated trials.
weaknesses: Several principal complexity statements are formally false because they omit an additive constant per access. Since depth is defined to include the accessed vertex, it cannot be O(log(1/w_x)) when w_x approaches one. For example, with frequencies (m-1,1), the claimed O(mH(p)) cost is O(log m), although any tree requires at least m comparisons. The correct form is O(1+log(1/w_x)) and O(m(1+H(p))); the same issue propagates to the B-Tree, robustness, and dynamic statements.

The weight-update guarantee is not established. Corollary 2.7 and Theorem C.2 claim O(|log(w'/w)|) work, but the offered delete-and-reinsert argument gives O(log(1/w)+log(1/w')), while the discontinuous tier boundaries require a separate analysis. The dynamic theorems rely directly on this unsupported bound.

The working-set result has a serious timing/indexing gap. The score work(i,x) depends on accesses after time i, and the algorithm updates x's priority before charging the lookup depth, implicitly requiring a pointer to the node before it has been found. The priority present before an access corresponds to the preceding score, not work(i,x). A shifted total-cost result may be recoverable, but the claimed per-access working-set guarantee is not proved as written.

The B-Treap extension is only a proof sketch. It does not verify B-Tree occupancy/branching invariants after joining tier components, rigorously justify applying the cited high-probability result simultaneously across components, or explain how weight changes maintain the decomposition. Consequently, the principal external-memory claims are not presently reproducible or convincing.

Some robustness results are incorrect. In Corollary C.6, a lower bound on p_x is incorrectly used as a lower bound on q_x; an L-infinity bound permits q_x to be arbitrarily small when the error is comparable to p_x. Corollaries C.7-C.9 inherit this problem. Moreover, the text repeatedly calls the KL overhead 'exactly' m times the divergence, whereas the analysis supplies only an asymptotic upper bound on cost.

The experiments contain an unexplained internal contradiction. Under the stated perfect uniform-frequency setup, all learned-Treap keys occupy one tier and receive i.i.d. uniform offsets, making the resulting tree distribution identical to a randomized Treap. Nevertheless, Figure 4 reports a large advantage for the proposed method, casting doubt on the implementation or accounting.

The empirical evidence does not test the dynamic working-set method or the proposed B-Treap in an external-memory setting. It uses only synthetic workloads and key comparisons, omitting update, construction, prediction, memory, and block-I/O costs. The KL experiment also changes workloads as divergence changes, all baseline costs move substantially, and no fit or statistical test supports the asserted linear relationship. Code, seeds, hardware, error-bar definitions, and sufficient optimizer details are absent.

The novelty and significance are not sharply positioned against classical weighted/near-optimal search-tree constructions or against splay trees, which already provide a working-set guarantee without future predictions. Numerous notation and presentation inconsistencies, including mutually reversed inequalities and mislabeled quantities in Figure 7, further impede verification. Overall, the static construction is promising, but errors and gaps affecting multiple headline conclusions make rejection more appropriate at present.

strengths: The static construction is simple and insightful: log-log weight tiers combined with independent random tie-breaking. The tier-cardinality and harmonic-ancestor argument supports an expected depth of O(1 + log(1/w_x)) for arbitrary positive weights.
The cross-entropy viewpoint provides a useful way to express an upper bound under inaccurate frequency predictions and connects naturally to KL divergence.
The manuscript is broadly well organized and ambitiously considers binary trees, external-memory B-trees, prediction robustness, and temporal locality.
weaknesses: A central update guarantee is false. Weights can straddle a log-log tier boundary while w'/w is arbitrarily close to one; the integer priority then changes by one and an endpoint can rotate past Theta(log |S_t|) same-tier ancestors. Thus the cost cannot be O(|log(w'/w)|). Deleting and reinserting only yields a sum-of-depths bound. This invalidates Corollary 2.7, Theorem C.2(3), and the stated proofs of the dynamic and dynamic-robustness results.

The working-set theorem is not established in a coherent operational model. work(i,x) depends on the next, future occurrence; before request i the tree contains the previous priority, but the theorem bounds the current lookup using the newly assigned priority without specifying whether searching or updating happens first. Its proof simply invokes the invalid update analysis. Moreover, the large-B assumption excludes ordinary BSTs despite broader BST claims.

The static statements omit necessary additive terms. Because depth is defined as the number of vertices on the search path, O(log(1/w_x)) is impossible as w_x approaches one; the valid form needs O(1 + log(1/w_x)), and total cost needs an additive Omega(m). Likewise, the paper derives only a cross-entropy upper bound, not the claimed exact or necessarily linear increase in actual cost with KL divergence.

The B-tree appendix contains major gaps and incorrect robustness claims. An upper bound on C_t does not imply the asserted B=O(sqrt(C_t)) condition used for the high-probability argument. More decisively, an L-infinity bound on p-q gives no lower bound on q_x: a positive-mass item with p_x at most epsilon can have arbitrarily tiny q_x, making p_x log(1/q_x) unbounded. Therefore Corollary C.6 and its L2, total-variation, and Hellinger corollaries do not follow.

The experiments are internally inconsistent. Under uniform weights, the proposed Treap has constant-plus-i.i.d.-uniform priorities and hence exactly the same distribution as a randomized Treap, yet Figure 4 reports a large persistent gap. For n=1000 uniform keys and m=20000 accesses, any binary search tree needs roughly 180000 successful-search comparisons even in the optimal static shape, whereas the reported totals are only about 20000-35000. This indicates an erroneous metric or implementation.

The evaluation does not test the B-tree or dynamic contributions, uses only synthetic workloads, does not adequately specify the prediction-error construction, and provides no implementation details or code sufficient to diagnose the contradictory results. The novelty discussion also needs comparison with classical weighted or biased randomized search trees, which already target logarithmic access in inverse key weight.

strengths: The composite priority based on logarithmic weight tiers and randomized tie-breaking is simple and intuitive. The ancestor-count argument appears capable of proving the useful corrected bound O(1 + log(1/w_x)).
The attempt to treat static frequencies, prediction errors, temporal locality, BSTs, and external-memory B-trees within one framework is ambitious and relevant.
The manuscript provides a helpful overview, formal definitions, broad prior-work coverage, and extensive appendices. Entropy and cross-entropy are natural quantities for this problem.
weaknesses: The central static bounds are false as stated. Since depth counts vertices/comparisons, it is at least one, whereas O(log(1/w_x)) tends to zero as w_x approaches one. For two keys with frequencies m-1 and 1, the claimed O(mH(p)) total is only O(log m), although the m searches cost at least m. The necessary bounds are O(1+log(1/w_x)) and O(m(1+H(p))); this affects Theorems 2.4, 2.8, 2.13 and their B-tree analogues.

The update guarantees are not established. Corollary 2.7 and Theorem C.2(3) claim O(|log(w'/w)|) rotations or touched nodes, but deletion followed by insertion gives a sum of depths, not this difference. Moreover, an arbitrarily small weight change can cross a quantized tier boundary and cause nontrivial restructuring. The dynamic results rely on this unsupported claim and sometimes resample the random offset without charging for the resulting changes.

The working-set theorem has an unresolved timing/model inconsistency. work(i,x(i)) uses the interval from the current access to the next one and changes at the current access, while the lookup occurs in a tree carrying the previous priority. The claimed pointwise depth therefore requires promoting an item before locating it, or free direct pointers that would undermine the search model. A reindexed amortized result may be possible, but it is not what is proved.

The B-tree argument is only a sketch. It does not rigorously justify combining separately constructed tier B-treaps while preserving all invariants and operation costs, invokes B=O(C_t^{1/2}) without deriving it from the assumptions, and does not supply the concentration/union argument needed for the stated high-probability guarantees over operations.

The robustness claims are overstated. Theorem 2.13 provides an asymptotic cross-entropy upper bound, not an exact additive overhead of m times the KL divergence. Corollary C.6 incorrectly infers a lower bound on q_x from an L-infinity bound; q_x may be arbitrarily small or zero, invalidating C.6 and the corollaries derived from it.

Several probability claims are unsupported: Lemma 2.2 states a high-probability result but proves only an expectation, and statements about all guarantees holding with probability 1-delta omit their dependence on the sequence length and number of updates.

The empirical results are internally inconsistent with the stated setup. The paper alternately describes the x-axis as unique items and accesses while claiming n=1000 is fixed. More seriously, for a uniform distribution with n=1000 and m=20000, the plotted totals of roughly 20000-35000 comparisons are far below the roughly m log2(n) comparisons required by any BST, so the figures cannot represent the stated total access cost. The KL experiment is underspecified and confounds changing workloads with prediction error, and no dynamic or proposed B-tree experiment, optimal-static-tree baseline, real workload, or code artifact is provided.

The clearest surviving contribution is a simple construction for a classical static-optimality objective. Its significance relative to existing optimal static trees, weighted randomized trees, and oracle-free working-set guarantees of self-adjusting trees is not sufficiently established to compensate for the invalid or incomplete central claims.

strengths: The central composite-priority construction is elegant and simple: log-log weight tiers plus random offsets give a concise argument for per-key expected depth O(log(1/w_x)) beyond the Zipfian setting considered by the main cited predecessor. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-xgbakut1/call-1c9352fab3c142b89dc39e442b1c1f8d/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The counterexamples for raw-frequency and single-log priority assignments help motivate the particular construction.
Connecting prediction error to cross-entropy/KL divergence is natural and interpretable, while the proposed extensions to B-Trees and working-set locality are potentially significant.
The paper is generally readable and includes comparisons across Zipfian, uniform, adversarial, and corrupted-prediction settings with several learned and classical baselines.
weaknesses: A central update guarantee is unsupported and appears false as stated. Theorem C.2(3) and Corollary 2.7 claim cost O(|log_B(w'/w)|), but the supplied delete-and-reinsert argument yields O(log_B(1/w)+log_B(1/w')). Moreover, weights can cross a discrete log-log tier boundary while w'/w approaches one, so the claimed bound approaches zero although restructuring is required. The dynamic theorems explicitly rely on this result.

The B-Treap construction is only sketched. The paper does not establish that separately converting maximal same-tier subtrees and then “combining” them preserves B-Tree occupancy and structural invariants, nor does it explain how component splits and merges are maintained under updates. The operation and high-probability guarantees therefore do not follow convincingly from the cited B-Treap lemma.

The dynamic access model is ambiguous. For the accessed key, work(i,x(i)) is defined using its next access, while locating and updating the node must occur in the pre-update tree. The proof instead applies a post-update depth bound and leaves unstated whether future information and direct node pointers are available. Consequently, the claimed per-access working-set guarantee is not established for a standard search-tree operation.

The dynamic robustness statements assert cost(X,predicted)=cost(X,true)+O(error), but their proofs only compare analytical upper bounds. An upper bound on the true-score construction cannot be substituted for its actual cost without a matching lower bound; the justified conclusion would instead be an upper bound in terms of the true-score proxy plus error.

Formal boundary issues further weaken the claims: depth is alternately defined as vertices and ancestors, the access bounds omit the unavoidable additive one per lookup (or m in total), and the priority is undefined at w=1. Several auxiliary robustness and permutation arguments are also incomplete or incorrect at terminal accesses.

The evaluation covers only synthetic, static BST workloads. It does not test the proposed B-Treap, dynamic updates, working-set behavior, external-memory I/O, or real learned predictions. Equal KL divergence can represent very different error patterns, and the asserted linear trend is not supported by a fit or uncertainty analysis. Implementation details and code are insufficient for reproducing the comparisons.

The novelty discussion is concentrated on one recent learned Treap and does not adequately distinguish the static construction from the broader literature on weighted or biased randomized search trees. Given the solid static idea but substantial gaps in the main B-Tree and dynamic conclusions, rejection is presently more appropriate.

strengths: The tiered-priority construction is simple and insightful. Its main BST argument convincingly explains how randomization within weight tiers yields expected depth roughly logarithmic in inverse weight for arbitrary distributions, extending the Zipfian-specific analysis of Lin et al.
The counterexamples for two natural alternative priority assignments help motivate the unusual double-logarithmic transformation.

The paper ambitiously connects static optimality, external-memory B-trees, dynamic locality, and prediction robustness within one framework. The cross-entropy/KL upper bound in the static setting is useful.
The manuscript is well organized, provides substantial appendices, and evaluates several classical and learning-augmented baselines with repeated trials and prediction-noise settings.
weaknesses: A major claimed update bound is not established and appears false. Corollary 2.7 and Theorem C.2 claim O(|log(w'/w)|) rotations or touched nodes, but deleting and reinserting only gives O(log(1/w)+log(1/w')). Weights can straddle a tier boundary while w'/w is arbitrarily close to one, yet the integer priority changes by a full tier and can cross many ancestors. The dynamic proofs rely on this bound; moreover, their newly sampled delta at every update can change the priority even within one tier.

The working-set theorem has an access-order mismatch. At time i, work(i,x(i)) measures the interval from the current occurrence to the next one and therefore uses future accesses. Before x(i) is found, however, the tree contains its previous priority; updating first would require an uncharged pointer or search. A shifted, update-after-access argument may be possible, but the stated per-access guarantee and the claimed standard working-set property do not follow from the presented proof.

The dynamic robustness results are unsupported. The proofs infer cost(X,predicted)=cost(X,true)+O(error) from separate big-O upper bounds, which cannot be subtracted in this way. Deterministic tier boundaries also make tree structure discontinuous under arbitrarily small log-weight errors, contradicting the claimed MAE-style smooth degradation without an additional argument or randomized boundaries.

Several static statements are formally false as written because they omit the unavoidable unit access cost: depth should be O(1+log(1/w)), and total cost should include an additive m. Consequently, the entropy-only quantity called OPT can be smaller than the actual optimum for highly concentrated distributions. Likewise, the text's claim that actual overhead is exactly m times KL divergence overstates Theorem 2.13, which only supplies an asymptotic total-cost upper bound.

Some auxiliary robustness claims are incorrect. In Corollary C.6, an L-infinity bound does not prevent a predicted probability q_x from being arbitrarily close to zero, so cross-entropy cannot be bounded by the displayed expression without clipping or a lower bound on q_x. Corollaries derived from it inherit this problem.

The B-tree extension needs substantially more justification: connecting separately constructed same-tier B-Treaps is not shown to preserve all B-tree invariants, the asserted relation B=O(sqrt(C_t)) does not follow from the upper bound on C_t, and the high-probability and update guarantees are largely asserted rather than proved.

The empirical evidence is too limited for the breadth of the claims. It uses only small synthetic static-frequency workloads and comparison counts; the dynamic working-set method, learned B-Treap, update costs, realistic predictors, wall-clock performance, and real workloads are not evaluated. The SLSQP construction of distributions at a prescribed KL value is under-specified, and Figure 6 does not by itself confirm that actual overhead is linear in KL.

The relationship to classical biased or weighted randomized search trees/treaps is not adequately discussed. Since such structures also target logarithmic inverse-weight access bounds, this omission makes the originality and comparative advantage of the central static construction difficult to assess.

strengths: The composite-priority construction is simple and conceptually appealing. Grouping weights into double-logarithmic tiers and randomizing within tiers gives a largely clear argument for weight-sensitive expected depth over arbitrary distributions, extending the Zipfian-only analysis emphasized in prior work.

The paper pursues a useful collection of objectives: static optimality, prediction-error guarantees, dynamic updates, and an external-memory extension. The entropy/cross-entropy viewpoint provides an intuitive connection between prediction quality and search cost.
The counterexamples for two alternative priority assignments help motivate why neither deterministic frequency priorities nor the more direct single-logarithmic bucketing is sufficient in general.
The manuscript is broadly well organized, and the proof of the central within-tier ancestor bound is concise and understandable.
weaknesses: The claimed weight-update bound is not established and appears false. Deleting and reinserting a node gives a cost depending on log(1/w)+log(1/w'), not |log(w'/w)| as asserted in Theorem C.2. More fundamentally, an arbitrarily small multiplicative weight change can cross a floor-induced tier boundary and move a node past an entire tier, requiring Theta(log n) rotations while |log(w'/w)| tends to zero. Resampling the random offset on updates creates a similar problem even within one tier. The dynamic-cost proofs rely directly on this unsupported bound, so the working-set and prediction-update conclusions are not currently proved.

Several central asymptotic statements omit the unavoidable additive unit search cost. Expected depth O(log(1/w_x)) is impossible as w_x approaches one, and total successful-search cost cannot generally be O(m H(p)), which may be o(m). The corresponding B-tree formulas have the same problem and should contain terms such as 1+log(1/w_x) and m(1+H_B(p)). Consequently, the claimed constant-factor match to the static optimum is not correct as written.

The robustness discussion overstates what is shown. The analysis provides an upper bound involving cross entropy; it does not prove that the actual additional cost is exactly, or even lower bounded linearly by, m times the KL divergence. The dynamic robustness proofs also replace an upper bound for the true-score structure by its actual cost without establishing the required comparison. Moreover, the L-infinity robustness proof incorrectly assumes that an item with small true probability has O(log_B n) depth under an arbitrary predicted probability; without a lower bound on that prediction, it may be arbitrarily smaller than the truth.

The empirical results fail basic sanity checks. Under uniform predicted frequencies, all proposed priorities lie in one tier with i.i.d. uniform offsets, making the proposed BST distributionally identical to an ordinary randomized Treap, yet Figure 4 reports a large systematic advantage. With n=1000 and m=20000 uniform accesses, the plotted totals of roughly 20000–35000 comparisons imply near-one comparison per query, impossible for uniform successful searches in a 1000-key BST. The stated fixed n and varying m also conflict with the description of the x-axis.

The prediction-error experiments do not convincingly isolate prediction error: even prediction-independent structures change dramatically with KL divergence, suggesting that workload difficulty is changing simultaneously. Figures 5 and 6 claim the same setup but report substantially different costs for the proposed method. The optimizer target, error-bar definition, implementation details, and code are absent, preventing reproduction.

The B-tree construction and high-probability claims need substantially more justification. The proof merely states that independently built tier B-Treaps can be combined, without verifying all structural and update invariants, and it conflates a constant probability 1-delta with a high-probability guarantee. The dynamic result additionally requires B=Omega(log^1.1 n), so it does not establish the repeatedly suggested binary-search-tree working-set result. Exact future working-set information is also a strong oracle, while classical self-adjusting trees already achieve working-set bounds without such advice.

strengths: The composite priority construction is simple and conceptually appealing. The tier-counting argument gives a reasonably clear route to an expected O(1 + log(1/w_x)) static depth bound for arbitrary weight distributions, improving the stated scope over frequency-only priorities.

The entropy and cross-entropy viewpoint provides an interpretable connection between prediction quality and static search cost. The counterexamples for two alternative priority assignments are also useful motivation.
The paper ambitiously considers binary trees, external-memory B-trees, dynamic priorities, and prediction robustness, and it includes substantial appendices containing the attempted proofs.
The manuscript is generally organized around explicit definitions and theorem statements, and the figures are visually legible.
weaknesses: The dynamic results rely on an unproved and apparently false update bound. Theorem C.2 claims that changing a weight from w to w' costs O(|log_B(w'/w)|), but its proof merely invokes deletion followed by insertion, which yields a bound depending on log_B(1/w) + log_B(1/w'), not their difference. Moreover, Appendix D redraws an independent random offset at each update; an arbitrarily small within-tier weight change can therefore substantially rearrange a large same-tier treap while the claimed bound tends to zero. Theorems D.1, D.5, and D.10 consequently lack support.

The claimed working-set property has an indexing and causality problem. At an access to x at time i, the definition uses prev(i,x)=i, so work(i,x) measures distinct future items until the next access, whereas the tree before the current update stores the score from the preceding interval. The paper neither specifies an operational search/update order nor accounts for locating the node before changing its priority. Undefined first accesses and reliance on future information create additional gaps, so the standard causal working-set guarantee is not established.

Several robustness claims do not follow mathematically. From separate big-O upper bounds, Theorems D.2 and D.11 infer cost(X,predicted)=cost(X,true)+O(error), which requires a lower bound or coupling that is not provided. Corollaries C.6-C.9 are false without clipping or a lower bound on predicted probabilities: small L-infinity, L2, total-variation, or Hellinger error can still assign an arbitrarily tiny probability to a low-mass true item, making log(1/q_x) unbounded. The text also repeatedly describes the KL overhead as exact although only an upper bound is shown.

The reported experiments appear incompatible with elementary BST lower bounds. In the uniform experiment with n=1000 and m=20000, Figure 4 reports roughly 20000-35000 total comparisons, below two comparisons per query; even an optimally shaped BST under uniform accesses requires about 8.99 comparisons per successful search, or about 180000 total. Additionally, equal uniform weights make the proposed priorities identically distributed to those of a randomized treap, yet the figure reports a large advantage. These contradictions undermine the empirical conclusions and suggest an incorrect cost implementation or mislabeled metric.

Evaluation coverage is inadequate for the paper's main scope. There are no experiments for dynamic priorities, the working-set result, updates, B-trees, external-memory/cache behavior, or real access traces. The static experiments use only synthetic distributions; baseline configurations, the meaning of error bars, prediction-generation details, and code availability are insufficiently documented. The text also says the x-axis is the number of unique items although n is fixed and the plotted variable is m.

The B-tree extension is not established rigorously. The paper does not prove that combining separately maintained per-tier B-Treaps preserves all required B-tree invariants and operation bounds, and the proof glosses over small tier components and the conditions needed to apply the cited B-Treap lemma. The advertised general B-tree result also hides a polylogarithmic lower bound on B and an incompletely specified parameter α.

Even the static statements contain formal errors. Lemma 2.2 claims every node has depth Θ(log n) with high probability, which is false for the root, while its proof establishes only an expectation. Bounds such as O(log(1/p_x)) and O(mH(p)) omit the necessary additive constant: for p_x approaching one, a successful search still costs at least one comparison, and for a two-key highly skewed distribution mH(p) can be far below the unavoidable Θ(m) total cost.

The novelty discussion is incomplete. The construction is not adequately compared with classical biased or weighted randomized search trees and exponential-race/Gumbel-style weighted priority schemes that naturally target O(log(W/w_x)) depths. Given that the most convincing part is the static weighted-depth argument, this omission makes the originality and significance difficult to assess.

There are numerous additional rigor and presentation problems: prev is undefined before a key's first occurrence; the claimed permutation argument fails when multiple keys have no future occurrence; Figure 7's caption reverses inequalities stated in its proof; the initialization in Appendix D does not realize the assumed score vector; and several high-probability statements conflate a constant probability 1-δ with probability tending to one. Collectively, these are too extensive for a minor revision.

strengths: The composite priority construction is simple and insightful. Stratifying keys by predicted weight and randomizing within tiers yields a clear argument for expected depth controlled by log(1/w), extending the stated Zipfian-only approach to arbitrary distributions.

The entropy and cross-entropy viewpoint provides an intuitive connection between prediction quality and search cost. The counterexamples for simpler priority assignments also motivate the double-log bucketing.
Extending the framework toward external-memory B-Trees, time-varying scores, and working-set behavior is ambitious and potentially significant.
The empirical section compares against several learned and classical structures, reports multiple distributions and prediction-error levels, and averages over independent trials.
weaknesses: A central update guarantee is unsupported and appears false as stated. Corollary 2.7 and Theorem C.2 claim O(|log(w'/w)|) restructuring, but deletion followed by insertion only gives a bound depending on log(1/w)+log(1/w'). Moreover, an arbitrarily small weight change can cross a discrete tier boundary, while the claimed bound tends to zero. The dynamic and general time-varying results rely on this assertion.

Many formal cost bounds omit an unavoidable additive constant per access. Since depth is defined as the number of vertices on the root-to-key path, O(log(1/p_x)) is impossible when p_x=1 and O(mH(p)) can be o(m) for concentrated distributions. The statements require 1+log(1/p_x), or an additive m term; the same issue affects the B-Tree, robustness, and working-set bounds.

The claimed working-set property is not established in the conventional causal sense. The score uses the interval until the next access, whereas the standard per-access bound uses distinct keys since the previous access. The operational timing and oracle information must be specified and the indices shifted appropriately. The supporting proof also incorrectly says interval sizes form a permutation near the end of a finite sequence, and Figure 7 reverses several inequalities and locality statements.

The B-Treap extension is too sketchy for its importance. The paper does not rigorously verify that combining tier-wise B-Treaps preserves the required B-Tree invariants, and it invokes B=O(C_t^{1/2}) without justification from the stated upper bound on C_t. Expected and high-probability conclusions are also conflated.

The experiments do not validate the dynamic or external-memory contributions and use only small synthetic workloads and comparison counts. More seriously, under uniform predicted weights the proposed priorities are distributed exactly like ordinary randomized-Treap priorities, yet Figure 4 shows a large systematic advantage over that baseline. This requires an implementation-level explanation or correction and currently undermines the empirical evidence.

The positioning against classical weighted or biased randomized search trees is insufficient to establish the novelty of the static result. Reproduction is further hindered by underspecified sequence generation, KL-constrained prediction construction, and implementation details. Overall, the static idea has merit, but the unsupported dynamic claims and experimental inconsistency make rejection more appropriate in the present form.

strengths: The composite priority construction is simple and intuitive. Grouping keys into doubly exponential weight tiers and randomizing within tiers gives a largely convincing route to entropy-sensitive expected depths for arbitrary weight distributions, extending the stated Zipfian-only baseline.
Connecting inaccurate frequency predictions to cross-entropy and KL divergence is natural and useful, once the bounds are stated with the necessary additive access cost.
The paper ambitiously develops one framework across BSTs, external-memory B-Trees, dynamic updates, and temporal locality, and the core BST argument is relatively accessible and self-contained.
The empirical section includes multiple classical and learning-augmented baselines, several synthetic distributions, prediction-error experiments, and repeated trials.
weaknesses: The central bounds omit an unavoidable additive constant per access. Depth is explicitly the number of vertices on a root-to-key path, yet Theorem 2.4 claims O(log(1/w_x)), which approaches zero as w_x approaches one. For frequencies (m-1,1), Theorem 2.8's claimed total is O(log m), although at least m comparisons are necessary. The correct forms require O(1+log(1/w_x)) and O(m(1+H(p))). This also invalidates the stated interpretation that prediction overhead is exactly or linearly m times KL divergence; the proof establishes only an asymptotic upper bound.

The weight-update guarantee is unsupported and generally false as stated. Deleting and reinserting a key yields a bound involving log(1/w)+log(1/w'), not |log(w'/w)|. An arbitrarily small change across a quantized tier boundary can cause a constant expected number of rotations while |log(w'/w)| tends to zero. Corollary 2.7, Theorem C.2(3), and the dynamic analyses therefore require a new argument and corrected bounds.

The B-Treap proof has substantial gaps. It invokes B=O(C_t^{1/2}) for every tier without this following from the assumptions, misstates the tier-size bound, does not rigorously show that attaching independently constructed tier components preserves B-Tree invariants and update costs, and does not justify transferring component-level probability bounds to the entire structure. Calling probability 1-delta 'with high probability' is also incorrect when delta is fixed.

The dynamic access timing is unclear and potentially circular: the structure changes the queried key's priority before charging its new depth, but locating that key normally costs its old depth unless a direct pointer is assumed. Moreover, work(i,x) is defined using the next occurrence and therefore requires future information rather than being the standard past-based working-set quantity. A shifted update-after-access proof may be possible, but it is not supplied.

The significance of the dynamic result is insufficiently established because classical self-adjusting trees already attain a working-set bound without predictions. No actual predictor, causal proxy, dynamic experiment, or B-Treap/external-memory experiment is evaluated.

The empirical evidence is limited to small synthetic static workloads and comparison counts; construction, model inference, updates, memory behavior, real workloads, seeds, and sufficient implementation details are absent. Under the stated uniform distribution and perfect equal-frequency oracle, the proposed priorities have exactly the same distribution as a randomized Treap, yet Figure 4 shows a large systematic advantage. This unexplained discrepancy raises concerns about the protocol or implementations. The claimed linear KL relationship is also asserted without a fitted model or statistical test.

The novelty discussion omits closely related biased or weighted randomized search trees, including weight-dependent exponential/geometric priority constructions that appear capable of the same O(log(W/w_x)) depth guarantee. Given that static entropy optimality and working-set bounds are classical, a precise comparison is necessary to establish originality.

Several additional inconsistencies impede verification: Theorem 4.4 mixes log base 2 and base B, Lemma 2.2 claims a high-probability result while its appendix proves only expectation, Corollary C.5 cites itself, the interval sizes need not be a permutation when keys never recur, and Theorem D.11 mixes true and predicted scores in its displayed derivation.

strengths: The composite priority—coarse weight tiers combined with random tie-breaking—is simple and insightful. The ancestor-counting argument largely explains why, after an additive-constant correction, it yields entropy-sensitive access for arbitrary distributions rather than only Zipfian ones.

The paper pursues an ambitious unified treatment of static BSTs, external-memory trees, prediction robustness, and temporal locality. The cross-entropy/KL perspective is a natural way to express sensitivity to frequency predictions.
The counterexamples for two plausible alternative priority rules help motivate the particular log-log transformation.
The inverse-square working-set score and its intended constant-l1 property are conceptually elegant, and the manuscript is generally well organized with proofs placed in appendices.
weaknesses: Several central bounds are false as stated because they omit an additive constant. Depth is defined as the number of vertices on a root-to-node path and is therefore at least one, so O(log(1/w_x)) must be O(1+log(1/w_x)). For a distribution concentrated on one key, mH(p) can be o(m), whereas any implementation performs at least m comparisons. Consequently, the stated static-optimality and cross-entropy bounds in Theorems 2.4, 2.8, 2.13, and their B-tree analogues do not follow as written.

The claimed update cost O(|log_B(w'/w)|) is unsupported and generally incompatible with the floored tier function. An arbitrarily small weight change can cross a tier boundary and require a nonzero number of rotations or touched nodes while the claimed bound tends to zero. Delete-and-reinsert only yields a bound involving log_B(1/w)+log_B(1/w'), not their difference. The notation also suggests resampling the random offset on updates, which can reorder a same-tier subtree. These issues undermine the dynamic and prediction-robustness analyses that use the update claim.

The B-tree extension is not established rigorously. The proof applies the Golovin construction separately to same-tier components and asserts that they can be combined, without proving the resulting object satisfies the required B-tree structural constraints or operation costs. It also invokes B=O(C_t^{1/2}) despite having established only the upper bound C_t=O(B^{2^t}); small tiers directly violate that premise. The high-probability statements and their stated probability 1-delta are likewise not justified.

The dynamic working-set theorem has unresolved timing and indexing issues. work(i,x(i)) describes the interval until the next access, while the current search ordinarily occurs before x(i)'s priority can be updated; the paper does not specify the required pointer, update order, or oracle interface. Figure 7 incorrectly says that work is a permutation, reverses the work/interval inequality, and attributes local changes to the wrong quantity. A reindexed total-cost result may be possible, but the claimed per-access behavior is not proved.

The empirical results contain a decisive internal contradiction. Under the stated uniform distribution, all weights have the same tier, so learn-bst is exactly a randomized Treap up to an irrelevant additive priority constant; nevertheless Figure 4 reports a large systematic advantage. Moreover, with n=1000 uniform keys and m=20000 searches, any BST needs roughly 180,000 successful-search comparisons even when optimally balanced, whereas Figure 4 reports only about 20,000–35,000 while labeling the metric total comparisons. Thus either the implementation or the reported metric is inconsistent with the experimental description.

The experiments test only synthetic, static BST access workloads. They do not evaluate the proposed B-tree construction, dynamic working-set method, updates, oracle cost, or real traces. The SLSQP error-generation procedure, target distribution, error bars, and implementation details are insufficiently specified for reproduction.

The paper repeatedly interprets an asymptotic cross-entropy upper bound as an exact additive m times KL-divergence overhead; actual Treap cost does not equal that expression and may remain unchanged when predictions vary within a tier. Some additional robustness corollaries also require unstated lower bounds on predicted probabilities.

The novelty discussion omits directly relevant classical biased search trees and related weighted randomized search structures, which already seek logarithmic access in the inverse relative weight and support weight changes. This makes the incremental significance of the static construction difficult to assess.

strengths: The composite priority construction is simple and potentially useful. The ancestor-counting argument gives a largely convincing route to an arbitrary-weight expected-depth guarantee after a small additive correction, improving conceptually over the cited Zipf-only learned Treap.
The adversarial example clearly demonstrates why assigning raw frequencies as deterministic priorities can produce a linear-depth tree.
The paper ambitiously connects static optimality, external-memory trees, locality, and prediction-error measures, and compares against several classical and learning-augmented baselines.
weaknesses: The central bounds omit an unavoidable additive constant. Since depth is defined as the number of vertices on the search path, Theorem 2.4 cannot give O(log(1/w_x)) when w_x approaches one; the correct form is O(1+log(1/w_x)). Consequently, the total static cost and OPT definitions require an additive m term. This also affects the entropy and robustness claims.

The weight-update guarantee is unsupported and generally false as stated. Deleting and reinserting costs O(log_B(1/w)+log_B(1/w')), not O(|log_B(w'/w)|). Moreover, deterministic tier boundaries allow an arbitrarily small weight change to cause a whole-tier priority jump, while the dynamic construction additionally resamples the random offset. This step is repeatedly invoked in the dynamic results, leaving their presented proofs incomplete.

The robustness conclusions substantially overstate what is proved. Theorem 2.13 supplies only an upper bound involving cross-entropy; it does not imply that actual additional cost is exactly or linearly equal to m times KL divergence. Similar invalid substitutions of asymptotic upper bounds for actual costs occur in Theorem D.2. Corollary C.6 is false without a lower bound on predicted probabilities: q_x can approach zero while the stated L-infinity error remains bounded, making the access cost unbounded.

The B-Treap argument is only a sketch and contains a logical gap: an upper bound on the number C_t of tier-t items does not establish the asserted condition B=O(sqrt(C_t)) used for the high-probability result. Maintenance of the combined tier components and preservation of the required B-tree invariants are also not established adequately.

The working-set formulation has unresolved timing and causality issues. Its score uses the next access, and the score of x changes at the same time x is accessed, but the manuscript does not explain how x can be relocated before it is found. Thus the claimed per-access depth is based on a post-access/future interval rather than the usual interval since the previous access. Figure 7's caption also reverses the permutation and inequality statements used in its proof.

The experiments are internally inconsistent and do not permit reproduction. Section 5.1 simultaneously fixes n=1000, varies m, and says the x-axis is the number of unique items, while the plots label it as the number of accesses. Under the stated setup, Figure 4 reports roughly 21,000 comparisons for 20,000 uniform accesses to 1,000 keys, which is incompatible with the comparison cost of a BST. In Figure 5, prediction error changes the costs of prediction-independent baselines dramatically, indicating that input difficulty is confounded with prediction error. Error bars are undefined, implementation details and code are absent, and there are no experiments for the dynamic or proposed B-Treap results.

The originality discussion does not adequately distinguish the static construction from classical biased or weighted randomized search trees, including priorities based on weighted exponential races, which can also yield logarithmic depth in inverse weight. Since static near-optimal trees are already known, this comparison is important—especially because the more novel dynamic claims are not convincingly established.

strengths: The tiered composite-priority construction is simple and insightful. The mass-per-tier and randomized tie-breaking argument plausibly establishes an expected per-key depth of O(1 + log(1/w_x)) for arbitrary weight distributions, substantially generalizing the distribution-specific analysis of Lin et al.

The paper pursues an ambitious and potentially useful unification of weighted Treaps, external-memory B-Treaps, temporal locality, and prediction-error guarantees. The cross-entropy perspective provides an interpretable connection between prediction quality and access cost.

The adversarial example motivates why using raw frequencies as deterministic priorities can fail, and the experiments include several classical and learning-augmented baselines across Zipfian, uniform, adversarial, and noisy-prediction settings.
weaknesses: A central update guarantee is unsupported and appears false as stated. Corollary 2.7 and Theorem C.2(3) claim O(|log_B(w'/w)|) update cost, but deletion followed by insertion only gives a sum of the old and new depths. Moreover, an arbitrarily small weight change crossing a tier boundary changes the integral priority and can require nonconstant restructuring. The dynamic and working-set analyses rely directly on this guarantee, so their main conclusions are not established by the provided proofs.

The static depth and entropy bounds omit a necessary additive constant. If w_x approaches one, log(1/w_x) approaches zero although a successful search still performs at least one comparison. Consequently, O(m Ent(p)) and OPT=m Ent(p) are false under the paper's stated depth/comparison convention; the valid form is O(m(1+Ent(p))). This correction likely preserves constant-factor static optimality but invalidates several displayed claims.

The robustness conclusions overstate what is proved. Theorem 2.13 gives only an upper bound O(m Ent(p,q)); it does not imply that the actual additional cost equals, or even is upper-bounded solely by, m times the KL divergence, because one cannot subtract two unrelated big-O bounds. Similar equality-style reasoning appears in the dynamic robustness results.

The dynamic section contains further consequential inconsistencies: access depth is bounded using the newly updated, future-dependent score rather than the score present when the item is located; the proof uses log base 4 while the stated working-set priority uses log base 2; and Figure 7 reverses the permutation and inequality statements used in its proof. High-probability guarantees and their behavior over an entire update sequence are also not justified.

The experiments are insufficiently specified and appear internally inconsistent. With n=1000 and m=20000 uniform accesses, the plotted total comparison costs imply roughly 1–2 comparisons per search, which is impossible for uniform successful searches in a 1000-key BST. The text also confuses the number of accesses with the number of unique items, does not define error bars or the precise noisy-distribution construction, and provides no evaluation of the dynamic or B-Tree contributions.

The novelty discussion does not adequately distinguish the method from classical nearly optimal weighted BSTs and biased/randomized search-tree constructions. A direct comparison of guarantees, construction cost, and update support is needed to establish the significance of the specific composite-priority mechanism.

strengths: The core construction—bucketing weights on a log-log scale and randomizing priorities within tiers—is simple, intuitive, and potentially useful. The tier-counting and ancestor arguments provide a plausible route to static optimality for arbitrary distributions, improving on the cited Zipfian-only method.
The cross-entropy connection for inaccurate frequency predictions and the bounded-norm working-set score are useful conceptual insights.
The paper ambitiously connects static BSTs, external-memory B-trees, dynamic locality, and prediction robustness within one framework.
The adversarial examples illuminate weaknesses of directly using frequencies as priorities, and the empirical section includes several classical and learning-augmented baselines.
weaknesses: The basic bounds omit a necessary additive constant. Since depth is defined as the number of vertices on the search path, it is at least one, whereas log(1/w_x) can approach zero. The correct form is O(1+log(1/w_x)), giving total cost O(m(1+H(p))), not O(mH(p)). The analogous B-tree definition of OPT is likewise incorrect as stated.

The claimed update bound in Corollary 2.7 and Theorem C.2 is unsupported and generally false. An arbitrarily small weight change can cross a discretized tier boundary and promote a node through many same-tier ancestors, even though |log(w'/w)| approaches zero. Delete-and-reinsert yields a sum-of-depths bound, not the claimed log-ratio bound. The dynamic proofs rely on this claim and also resample random offsets, so the working-set and dynamic robustness results do not follow as written.

The B-tree extension is insufficiently justified. The proof applies Golovin's construction separately to tier components and then glues them together without establishing the resulting B-tree invariants or the costs of component merging, splitting, and updating. It also invokes conditions such as B=O(C_t^{1/2}) that need not hold, while the high-probability claims are not derived for an entire dynamic sequence.

Robustness is overstated. The cross-entropy identity concerns a bound, not the actual tree cost, so it does not establish that the realized overhead is exactly m times the KL divergence. Theorems D.2 and D.11 similarly turn one-sided big-O bounds into equalities relative to cost(X,w). Moreover, Corollaries C.6–C.9 are false without a lower bound on predicted probabilities: small L-infinity, total-variation, or Hellinger error still permits q_x to approach zero for p_x>0, making cross-entropy arbitrarily large.

The working-set development contains unresolved definition and proof issues: prev(i,x) is undefined before a key's first occurrence; interval sizes are not a permutation when several keys never reappear; and Figure 7's caption reverses the proved inequality and attributes locality to the wrong quantity. The per-access score also depends on the next occurrence rather than the conventional past working set, so the oracle-dependent and standard online guarantees should be distinguished carefully.

The experiments test only the static binary structure, leaving the B-tree, update, and dynamic claims unevaluated. They use small synthetic workloads and omit critical reproduction details such as tie handling, sequence construction, optimization objectives, and error-bar meaning. In the KL experiment, prediction-independent baselines change by severalfold as KL varies, suggesting that workload difficulty is changing along with prediction error; this prevents the plots from isolating robustness. Figure 6 shows only a noisy trend and cannot validate the claimed exact linear overhead.

The related-work discussion does not adequately distinguish the construction from classical biased or weighted randomized search trees, weakening the case for originality beyond the comparison with Lin et al.

The static KL-divergence analysis has a useful core insight: using predicted frequencies replaces entropy by cross-entropy, giving a natural degradation bound as prediction quality worsens.

The attempt to unify BSTs, external-memory B-Trees, and temporally adaptive trees is ambitious. In particular, the future working-set score and its constant-L1-norm argument are clever and potentially useful.

The paper is generally well organized and includes comparisons across Zipfian, uniform, adversarial, and noisy-prediction settings over ten trials. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-stpqubef/call-a3ff8994d1b146fc994faf40f739d2c4/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: A key update guarantee is not established. Corollary 2.7 and Theorem C.2(3) claim O(|log_B(w'/w)|) rotations or touched nodes, but the given delete-and-reinsert argument only yields a bound involving log_B(1/w)+log_B(1/w'). Moreover, the dynamic construction appears to draw a fresh random offset after an update, so an arbitrarily small weight change can alter relative priorities while the claimed bound tends to zero. The dynamic and prediction-robustness theorems rely on this sensitivity claim. A weaker bound may rescue the working-set result, but the current chain of results is incomplete.

The depth and static-cost statements omit an essential additive constant: they should be O(1+log(1/w_x)) and O(m(1+H(p))). As written, a distribution approaching a point mass gives mH(p)=o(m), although processing m accesses requires Omega(m) work under the paper's own depth/comparison convention. Consequently, OPT_static=mH(p) and the claim that the prediction overhead is exactly m times KL divergence are not valid as stated.

The B-Treap extension is supported mainly by a four-step construction sketch. It does not rigorously show that stitching independently represented tier components preserves all B-Tree invariants or that insertions, deletions, component splits/merges, and weight changes attain the stated costs. The simultaneous high-probability guarantees are also not derived, and the uses of alpha and delta are ambiguous; in several statements a fixed success probability 1-delta is called 'with high probability.'

Some additional theoretical claims are false or insufficiently justified. Lemma 2.2 states a high-probability result but proves only an expectation, and its literal claim about every node cannot hold because a root has constant depth. More seriously, Corollary C.6 assumes that q_x gives O(log_B n) depth whenever p_x is small, but an L-infinity error bound alone permits q_x to be arbitrarily close to zero; smoothing or a lower bound on q_x is required. The subsequent L2, total-variation, and Hellinger corollaries inherit this problem.

The advertised working-set guarantee is noncausal: at access i it uses the number of distinct items through the next occurrence of the key, whereas the standard online working-set bound uses accesses since the previous occurrence. The introduction says that predicting the next-access interval suffices, but the theorem needs a future distinct-item count and assumes a globally coherent, locally changing, bounded-L1 score vector. How a practical oracle provides these quantities is not explained or evaluated.

The empirical evidence does not cover most principal claims: there are no dynamic, update-cost, B-Treap, external-memory, or real-data experiments, and construction/reorganization and oracle costs are omitted. The static comparison lacks an optimal or nearly optimal weighted BST and relevant biased randomized-tree baselines. Prediction generation via SLSQP is underspecified, no reproducibility artifact is identified, and Figure 5 does not support the blanket claim of outperforming every alternative at the largest displayed error.

Because static optimality with known frequencies is classical, the related-work discussion needs a sharper comparison with classical biased/weight-sensitive randomized search trees and nearly optimal alphabetic BST constructions. strengths: The composite-priority idea is simple and insightful: doubly exponential weight tiers with random tie-breaking plausibly give the corrected expected-depth bound O(1 + log(1/w_x)) for arbitrary distributions, extending the Zipf-specific construction in prior work. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-rjiivovc/call-876373f1c5b0434aa287679b26c58b14/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The cross-entropy viewpoint provides a useful route to prediction-dependent upper bounds involving entropy and KL divergence, once the claims and missing baseline are corrected.
Using one priority mechanism for static Treaps, external-memory B-Treaps, and temporal-locality variants is elegant and potentially useful.

The evaluation includes several classical and learning-augmented baselines, multiple synthetic distributions, prediction noise, and repeated trials; the adversarial distribution directly probes a known weakness of frequency-only priorities.
weaknesses: The principal static theorem is false as stated because it omits an additive unit access cost. With frequencies (m-1,1), the claimed sum_x f_x log(m/f_x) is Theta(log m), although m successful searches require at least m comparisons under the paper's own vertex-depth definition. The correct statements require O(1 + log(1/w_x)) per key and O(m(1+H(p))) overall. This error propagates to the claimed static-optimal costs and the B-Tree definition of OPT.

The claimed weight-update bound O(|log(w'/w)|) is unsupported and generally false. An arbitrarily small multiplicative change crossing a tier boundary can move a key past many same-tier ancestors; resampling the random offset can also substantially restructure a tier. The appendix's delete-and-reinsert argument yields a sum-of-depths bound, not a log-ratio bound. Corollary 2.7, Theorem C.2(3), and the dynamic analyses relying on them therefore need substantial repair.

Robustness is overstated. Theorem 2.13 supplies only an upper bound proportional to cross-entropy; it does not show that actual excess cost is exactly, or even linearly equal to, m times KL divergence. The dynamic proofs similarly subtract big-O upper bounds as though they were actual costs. Moreover, the L-infinity result is false without a lower bound on predicted probabilities: q_x can approach zero while ||p-q||_infinity remains at most 1/n, making cross-entropy unbounded while Corollary C.6 predicts only O(m log_B 2); Corollaries C.7-C.9 inherit this problem.

The B-Treap extension is only a proof sketch. It invokes Golovin's component guarantee while asserting unproved component-size conditions, does not adequately justify the simultaneous high-probability result for small tiers, and gives insufficient detail that joining tier components preserves all B-Tree invariants and stated update costs.

The working-set construction uses future next-access information, but the timing of prediction, lookup, and priority update is not defined consistently: the current access is bounded using the new score even though changing that key's priority normally requires first locating it. The assumed predicted vectors must also remain locally changed and normalized, with no mechanism shown to ensure this. Consequently, the advertised online self-reorganization and dynamic robustness claims are not convincingly established.

The experiments cover only small synthetic static workloads. There are no real workloads, learned predictors, dynamic/working-set tests, B-Tree block-I/O tests, or update/runtime/memory measurements. The protocol is internally inconsistent about whether the x-axis varies accesses or unique items. If frequencies are truly uniform, the proposed priority distribution should equal that of a randomized Treap, yet Figure 4 reports a large separation. Error bars, SLSQP construction details, seeds, and code are unspecified, and Figure 6 contains no fit or statistical test supporting linearity.

Several additional correctness and presentation problems reduce confidence: Lemma 2.2 claims a high-probability result but proves only an expectation; the working-set appendix incorrectly calls interval sizes a permutation when multiple keys never reappear, while Figure 7 reverses the stated inequality; Corollary C.5 cites itself; and notation, logarithm bases, and theorem statements are frequently inconsistent. The paper also does not sharply distinguish its static construction from classical biased/randomized search-tree techniques.

strengths: The exponentially spaced weight tiers with independent random tie-breaking form a simple and intuitive Treap construction. The tier-cardinality and harmonic-ancestor argument provides a plausible route to logarithmic expected depth for arbitrary weight distributions, substantially broadening the Zipfian-only setting emphasized in the comparison work.
The manuscript addresses a meaningful learning-augmented data-structure problem and usefully connects frequency predictions, cross-entropy/KL error, external-memory B-Trees, and temporal locality.
The adversarial examples help explain why directly using frequencies, or using more finely separated deterministic tiers, can produce poor trees.
The paper is organized around explicit theorem statements and includes appendices covering the proposed extensions and experiments across several synthetic distributions.
weaknesses: The static guarantees omit an unavoidable additive unit cost. Depth is defined as the number of vertices on the root-to-key path, so it is at least one, whereas O(log(1/p_x)) approaches zero for a dominant key and is undefined at p_x=1. Consequently, the claimed O(m Ent(p)) cost can be smaller than m. The correct form is approximately O(1+log(1/p_x)) per key and O(m(1+Ent(p))) overall; this correction propagates through the static-optimality and robustness statements.

The claimed O(|log(w'/w)|) weight-update bound in Corollary 2.7 and Theorem C.2(3) does not follow from deletion and reinsertion, which instead costs roughly O(log(1/w)+log(1/w')). More seriously, an arbitrarily small multiplicative change can cross a discrete tier boundary and promote a key through an entire same-tier Treap, requiring many rotations. The dynamic proofs D.1 and D.10 rely directly on this unsupported claim, so the dynamic and working-set results are not established as written, even if a different amortized argument might salvage them.

Several robustness conclusions overstate the analysis. The cross-entropy calculation supplies an upper bound, not proof that the actual additional cost is exactly m times the KL divergence. The dynamic proofs similarly establish at most a one-sided upper bound, despite stating equality up to an additive error. Corollary C.6 is invalid because an L-infinity bound on p-q does not provide the asserted lower bound on q_x; q_x can be arbitrarily small. The subsequent L2, total-variation, and Hellinger corollaries therefore do not follow.

The B-Treap extension is only a proof sketch. It does not rigorously justify that combining independently formed tier components preserves all B-Tree invariants and update costs, nor does it establish the simultaneous high-probability guarantees across components and an operation sequence. Conditions involving B, alpha, and delta are also inconsistently stated.

The experiments contain a major internal inconsistency. Under the stated uniform experiment with 1,000 keys and 20,000 accesses, the reported totals of roughly 21,000–35,000 comparisons are far below the information-theoretic cost of uniformly searching a binary tree. Moreover, equal weights make the proposed Treap distribution identical to a conventional randomized Treap, yet Figure 4 reports a large performance difference. Figures 5 and 6 also claim the same setup but show substantially different costs at zero KL divergence. These observations require an audit of the implementation and metric before the empirical claims can be trusted.

The evaluation covers only static synthetic BST workloads. It does not test the B-Tree construction, update costs, dynamic working-set behavior, real traces, runtime, or memory use. Sequence generation, rounding of frequencies, optimizer objectives, and source code are insufficiently documented for reproduction.

The working-set score depends on the next future access and is not the conventional causal per-access working-set quantity; the relationship should be stated more carefully. Its proof also incorrectly says interval-set sizes form a permutation when multiple keys never appear again, and Figure 7 reverses key inequalities and locality statements.

strengths: The manuscript presents a simple and appealing composite-priority construction, and the tier-counting argument clearly explains why it should provide weight-sensitive depths of O(1+log(1/w_x)). :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-rxh7uipj/call-47f0b21e579245e2bb233ca656398352/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Relating inaccurate frequency predictions to cross-entropy and KL divergence is natural and potentially useful for learning-augmented data structures.
The extension toward external-memory trees is ambitious, and the working-set score and its constant-norm argument are clever ideas for capturing temporal locality.

The experiments include multiple classical and learning-augmented baselines, several distributions, prediction errors, and repeated trials; they offer encouraging evidence for the static BST implementation.
weaknesses: Several central bounds omit an unavoidable additive constant. Since every search touches at least one node, depth cannot be O(log(1/p_x)) when p_x approaches one, and total cost cannot be O(mH(p)) when H(p)=o(1). The claimed B-tree optimum and working-set costs can likewise be o(m), which is impossible. The appropriate forms require terms such as 1+log_B(1/p_x) and m+mH_B(p). This is repairable but invalidates many stated theorems and comparisons.

The update guarantees are not proved and appear false as written. Corollary 2.7 and Theorem C.2 claim O(|log(w'/w)|) work, yet the given delete-and-reinsert argument only supports a sum of old and new depths. Moreover, the floored tier function is discontinuous: an arbitrarily small weight change can cross a tier boundary, while the claimed bound tends to zero. The dynamic proofs rely directly on this unsupported update statement, and their use of freshly indexed random offsets would permit additional within-tier reordering.

The B-tree extension is too informal to establish its main claims. Partitioning a binary Treap, independently constructing B-Treaps, and gluing them is not shown to preserve the required B-tree structure or update complexity when tier components split or merge. The proof also asserts B=O(C_t^{1/2}) for every tier, which need not hold for small components, and derives high-probability guarantees without the required tail and union-bound analysis. Even Lemma 2.2 states a high-probability result but proves only an expectation.

Some robustness statements are mathematically overstated or incorrect. Theorem 2.13 provides only a big-O cross-entropy upper bound, not an exact KL increase in actual cost, and Theorem D.2 turns one-sided upper bounds into an equality relative to the oracle tree's cost. Corollary C.6 is false without a lower bound on q_x: L-infinity closeness allows q_x to be arbitrarily near zero for a low-mass item, making log(1/q_x) arbitrarily large. The subsequent L2, total-variation, and Hellinger corollaries inherit this problem.

The dynamic access model and timing are underspecified. The working-set score used for access i depends on the next occurrence, while a locally updated tree would normally search using the previous priority and update only after locating the item. The paper neither provides the necessary reindexing argument nor states whether direct node pointers are assumed; direct pointers would materially change the search-tree model.

The novelty relative to classical biased or weighted randomized search trees is unclear. Non-uniform random-priority Treaps are known to yield comparable O(1+log(W/w_x)) expected search bounds for arbitrary weights, but the manuscript discusses the original Treap literature only through uniform priorities and does not distinguish its principal static result from that line of work.

The evaluation does not test the B-tree, external-memory, dynamic working-set, or update-cost claims. It uses only synthetic static workloads and comparison counts, with insufficient implementation details, no real datasets, no definition of the error bars, and an under-specified SLSQP procedure for generating prediction errors. Thus it cannot resolve the theoretical concerns or support the manuscript's broader practical claims.

Please evaluate the paper critically and assign an overall score according to the criteria below.

Assess whether the principal claims follow from clear and convincing evidence, whether the methods and evaluation are appropriate to the problem, and whether relevant theoretical or empirical arguments are sound. Examine how the contribution relates to prior work, its originality and significance, and whether the presentation permits informed understanding and reproduction.

Evaluate contributions in relation to their stated objectives. Useful insights and well-motivated combinations can constitute contributions; an entirely new method is not required. Distinguish major issues affecting the research conclusions from minor corrections. Give reasons that explain the recommendation rather than merely listing attributes.

Assign an Overall Assessment (OA) score using only: 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5.

Rating scale:
1 = Reject
The submission's important weaknesses or insufficiently supported contribution prevent acceptance.

2 = Weak reject
The paper has substantive merits, but concerns make rejection the more appropriate recommendation at present.

3 = Weak accept
The merits support a preference for acceptance, while the concerns are substantial enough that rejection would also be defensible.

4 = Accept
The paper provides a convincing and adequately supported contribution whose strengths justify acceptance.

5 = Strong accept
The supported contribution and overall quality make a particularly strong case for acceptance.

Output Format

Provide your review in JSON format. Use a numeric value for oa and lists of text for strengths and weaknesses:

{"oa": <num>, "strengths": ["<text>"], "weaknesses": ["<text>"]}
