strengths: The composite-priority construction is simple and appealing. Random tie-breaking within doubly logarithmic weight tiers gives a reasonably clear route to frequency-sensitive expected depths for arbitrary distributions, modulo an additive-constant correction.
Relating imperfect frequency predictions to cross-entropy and KL divergence is intuitive and potentially useful, even though the paper overstates what the resulting upper bound establishes.

The paper pursues an ambitious unified treatment of binary trees, external-memory trees, dynamic access patterns, and prediction robustness, and includes comparisons with several classical and learning-augmented baselines.
weaknesses: Several basic static statements are false as written. Since depth counts vertices, it is at least one, whereas O(log(1/w_x)) approaches zero when w_x approaches one. Consequently, the appropriate access bound is of the form O(1+log(1/w_x)), and the total static benchmark is O(m(1+H(p))), not O(mH(p)). The informal treatment of negative tiers does not establish the claimed per-item result.

The B-tree extension is not convincingly proved. The argument that C_t=O(B^{2^t}) implies B=O(C_t^{1/2}) is invalid, and independently converting tier components into B-Treaps and stitching them together is not shown to preserve B-tree occupancy, arity, or efficient maintenance. The insertion, deletion, and high-probability claims therefore do not follow from the short argument provided.

The claimed weight-update cost O(|log_B(w'/w)|) is unsupported: deleting and reinserting a key gives a sum-of-depths bound, not a difference-of-log-weights bound. Moreover, the dynamic construction draws a fresh random offset after an update, which can reorder a key within a large tier even for an arbitrarily small weight change. The dynamic, working-set, and dynamic-robustness theorems all rely on this update bound.

The dynamic access model is underspecified and internally misaligned. The score work(i,x(i)) depends on the interval until the next future access and changes at the current access, but the tree before that access still has the preceding score. Thus the claimed per-access depth does not follow without reindexing and a precise search-versus-update order. The proofs also appear to require a direct pointer to the requested node, which would need to be stated and reconciled with the search-tree model.

The robustness discussion repeatedly turns an O(cross-entropy) upper bound into claims that actual overhead is exactly or linearly m times KL divergence. Those conclusions do not follow. Corollary C.6 is also false under only L-infinity error: a predicted probability can be arbitrarily small for a positive but rare event, so its asserted O(log_B n) depth under q is unjustified; the subsequent L2, total-variation, and Hellinger corollaries inherit this problem.

The experimental results are incompatible with the stated protocol. For n=1000 uniform keys, any binary search tree requires an average of order log n comparisons, so m=20000 accesses require on the order of hundreds of thousands of comparisons; Figure 4 reports only roughly 20000–35000. The text also says that n is fixed and m varies while describing the x-axis as the number of unique items. These contradictions make the empirical claims uninterpretable.

The evaluation covers only static synthetic workloads: there are no experiments for the dynamic working-set method or the proposed external-memory structure, no real workloads, and no block-I/O or runtime measurements. Important reproduction details—including the precise noisy-distribution construction, error-bar meaning, implementation parameters, and code—are absent.

The relationship to classical biased or weighted randomized search trees is not adequately discussed, leaving the originality of the valid static core unclear. Numerous additional inconsistencies, including an expectation-only proof for a stated high-probability lemma and reversed statements in Figure 7's caption, further reduce confidence. Overall, the supported static insight is insufficient to compensate for unsupported central theorems and unreliable evaluation.

strengths: The composite priority transformation is simple and intuitive. The static BST analysis through tier cardinalities and harmonic bounds on same-tier ancestors is a useful idea and is largely convincing after a small additive-constant correction.
The counterexamples to raw frequency priorities and to a more direct logarithmic bucketing scheme help motivate why both coarsening and random tie-breaking are needed beyond the Zipfian setting.

Relating predicted frequencies to cross-entropy and KL divergence is natural and potentially useful. The locally changing working-set score and its bounded-l1-norm argument are also interesting conceptual ingredients.
The manuscript communicates its main intuition clearly and compares against several learned and classical search structures over multiple synthetic distributions.
weaknesses: The claimed weight-update bound is unsupported and false as stated. Corollary 2.7 and Theorem C.2(3) claim O(|log_B(w'/w)|) work, but deletion followed by insertion only gives O(log_B(1/w)+log_B(1/w')). More decisively, arbitrarily close weights can straddle a tier boundary, changing the integral priority tier and causing the item to traverse a large same-tier component while |log_B(w'/w)| tends to zero. Resampling the random offset during updates exacerbates this problem. Several dynamic theorems invoke this bound, so their proofs require substantial repair.

The dynamic analysis also confuses the pre-update and post-update trees: an access at time i occurs while the item has its previous score, whereas the proof bounds its depth using w(i) after updating it. Reindexing and charging both old and new depths may salvage the locally dynamic total bound, but that amortized argument is not provided. The more general dynamic claims, where unaccessed items may change, are not similarly salvageable from the stated access term.

The B-tree extension is only a proof sketch. It does not establish that gluing independently constructed per-tier B-Treaps preserves all B-tree degree/occupancy and update invariants. Moreover, the proof incorrectly infers B=O(sqrt(C_t)) from an upper bound C_t=O(B^(2^t)), and the asserted high-probability guarantees are neither derived nor meaningfully quantified; 'with high probability 1-delta' is especially ambiguous.

Because depth is defined as the number of vertices on the search path, it is at least one. Thus O(log(1/w_x)) is false as w_x approaches one, and the total bounds omit the unavoidable additive m access cost. The correct form is O(1+log(1/w_x)) and O(m+sum_x f_x log(m/f_x)). This also affects the stated static-optimality and robustness formulations.

The robustness claims are overstated. Theorem 2.13 proves only an upper bound proportional to cross-entropy, not that the additional cost is exactly m times KL divergence. Corollary C.6 is false without a lower bound on predicted probabilities: for a small true probability p_x, an L-infinity-close q_x can still be arbitrarily tiny, making log(1/q_x) arbitrarily large. The dynamic results likewise write equality to the ideal predictor's actual cost where only separate big-O upper bounds have been shown.

Figure 4 is inconsistent with the stated algorithm. Under a perfectly uniform distribution, every key has the same deterministic tier, so learn-bst has iid uniform within-tier priorities and therefore exactly the same distribution over trees as random-treap. Their reported costs differ substantially, suggesting an implementation, labeling, or experimental-protocol error that undermines the empirical evidence.

The evaluation covers only small synthetic, static binary-tree workloads. There are no B-tree or external-memory experiments, dynamic updates, working-set workloads, real access traces, learned predictors, wall-clock measurements, memory results, or accounting for construction, rotations, and prediction cost. Reproduction is also hindered by the absence of code, hardware details, precise sequence generation, optimizer targets, and a definition of the error bars.

The novelty discussion is incomplete. In particular, the paper does not compare with classical biased/randomized search trees or weight-dependent exponential-race Treap priorities, which can also provide expected O(log(W/w_x)) access depth for arbitrary weights. Since arbitrary-distribution static optimality is already classical, the manuscript needs to explain what the composite construction adds relative to these methods.

Numerous technical inconsistencies further impede verification: Lemma 2.2's appendix proof establishes only expectation despite a high-probability statement; Figure 7's caption reverses the permutation and inequality claims used in its proof; Corollary C.5 cites itself; and several dynamic theorems contain inconsistent logarithm bases, indices, free variables, or missing parentheses. Overall, the static idea has merit, but the advertised update, B-tree, dynamic, robustness, and empirical conclusions are not sufficiently supported for acceptance in the present form.

strengths: The tiered composite priority is simple and appealing. The core argument—bounding each tier's population and using random tie-breaking to control ancestors—provides a useful route toward frequency-sensitive Treaps for arbitrary distributions.

The manuscript ambitiously connects static BSTs, external-memory B-Trees, prediction robustness, and temporal locality within one framework. The working-set score's bounded-norm observation is particularly interesting.
The paper is generally well organized, includes substantial appendices, and compares the static method with several learned and classical baselines.
weaknesses: Several central bounds are false as stated because they omit the unavoidable additive access cost. With frequencies (m-1,1), the claimed O(m Ent(p)) bound is O(log m), although processing m accesses requires at least m comparisons. Depth bounds need O(1+log(1/p_x)), total bounds need an additive m, and the analogous B-Tree bounds need at least one node touch per access.

The weight-update guarantee in Theorem C.2(3) is not proved: deleting and reinserting gives a cost based on the sum of the old and new depths, not O(|log_B(w'/w)|). An arbitrarily small weight change can also cross a deterministic tier boundary. The dynamic results rely directly on this unsupported claim, so their current proofs do not establish the stated guarantees.

The B-Treap construction is too abbreviated to verify. It does not rigorously justify that gluing independently formed per-tier B-Treaps preserves all required invariants, and it invokes size conditions that need not hold for small tier components. Several robustness corollaries are also invalid without clipping or lower-bounding predicted probabilities; an L-infinity-close prediction may assign zero or arbitrarily small mass to an accessed item.

The working-set score uses the next future access, is undefined for items without a previous occurrence, and leaves the ordering of lookup versus priority update unclear. Since classical self-adjusting trees obtain working-set bounds causally, the manuscript needs a sharper explanation and evaluation of what predictive advice adds.

The evaluation covers only static synthetic BST workloads. It does not test the B-Tree, dynamic, update-cost, or working-set contributions, nor real workloads. The inaccurate-oracle generation procedure is under-specified and appears to vary workload characteristics along with KL divergence, so it does not cleanly isolate prediction error. Reproduction details and code are also absent, while claims of linear degradation exceed what the theory and plots establish.

Related-work positioning is insufficient against classical biased or frequency-aware randomized search trees, making the originality of the static result difficult to assess. Numerous inconsistencies—such as an expectation calculation presented as a high-probability proof and reversed statements in Figure 7's caption—further reduce confidence.

The paper pursues a coherent and potentially valuable unification of weighted BSTs, external-memory B-Trees, dynamic temporal locality, and prediction-error guarantees. Cross-entropy/KL error and working-set locality are natural performance measures.
The counterexamples to two naive deterministic/tiered priority assignments help motivate the double-logarithmic bucketing choice.
The presentation is generally accessible, and the experiments attempt broad comparison against both classical and learning-augmented baselines under perfect, adversarial, and inaccurate predictions.

With depth defined as the number of vertices on the search path, Theorem 2.4 cannot give O(log(1/w_x)) when w_x approaches one. For frequencies (m-1,1), the claimed total O(sum_x f_x log(m/f_x)) is O(log m), although m successful searches require at least m comparisons. The correct form is O(1+log(1/w_x)) and O(m+sum_x f_x log(m/f_x)); the B-Tree claims have the analogous issue.

The weight-update guarantee O(|log_B(w'/w)|) in Corollary 2.7 and Theorem C.2 is unsupported and generally false. The proofs of D.1 and D.10 invoke this false bound directly, so the dynamic, working-set, and dynamic-robustness results are not established as written. Their total bounds may be repairable using an amortized reindexing argument, but that argument is absent. The robustness conclusions are overstated. Theorem 2.13 proves only an asymptotic upper bound by cross-entropy, not that the additional cost is exactly m times KL divergence. Likewise, D.2/D.11 replace an upper-bound expression for the ideal tree by its actual cost, which does not follow from the preceding theorem. The L-infinity proof also assumes that a small true probability implies log_B(1/q_x)=O(log_B n), which fails when q_x is arbitrarily small or zero.

strengths: The composite-priority construction is simple and well motivated. The tier-cardinality and harmonic-ancestor arguments convincingly establish the core binary-Treap bound, modulo a necessary additive constant, and extend the prior Zipfian-specific approach to arbitrary weight distributions.
Expressing performance under estimated frequencies through cross-entropy and KL divergence is natural and gives a useful interpretation of prediction quality.

The paper ambitiously connects static optimality, external-memory search trees, dynamic locality, and prediction robustness within one framework. The future-gap score is an interesting way to make only the accessed key's priority change.

The manuscript is organized clearly, includes substantial appendices, motivates alternative priority choices with lower-bound examples, and compares against several classical and learning-augmented baselines.
weaknesses: Several principal theorem statements omit an essential unit-cost term. The claimed O(log(1/w_x)) depth should be O(1+log(1/w_x)), and total comparison cost should be O(m(1+H(p))) rather than O(mH(p)). For example, with frequencies (m-1,1), mH(p)=Theta(log m), although m successful searches require at least m comparisons. The same issue affects the B-tree and cross-entropy statements. Moreover, KL divergence is the exact difference between entropy expressions, not between the actual tree costs, for which only big-O upper bounds are proved.

The weight-update guarantee in Corollary 2.7 and Theorem C.2(3) is unsupported and appears false. Deleting and reinserting a key costs a sum of depths, not O(|log(w'/w)|). Because the priority uses a floor, arbitrarily close weights on opposite sides of a tier boundary can change the priority by a full tier and induce an unbounded number of rotations while |log(w'/w)| tends to zero; resampling the random offset makes the claim even less plausible. The dynamic analyses invoke this guarantee and therefore require a new proof, although a weaker amortized argument may be possible.

The B-Treap proof is not sufficiently rigorous. Its tier-size claim C_t=O(B^(2^t)) does not follow from the tier definition—the immediate bound has exponent 2^(t+1)—and the size/branching assumptions needed to apply the cited B-Treap lemma to every tier component are not verified. Construction invariants, small and negative tiers, union bounds, and the claimed high-probability guarantees are also left unclear; calling probability 1-delta 'with high probability' is nonstandard when delta is fixed.

The working-set result uses the number of distinct future requests before the next occurrence, rather than the standard causal, previous-access working-set quantity. The aggregate sums may be shift-equivalent, but the pointwise guarantee is different and requires a strong clairvoyant oracle. No implementable predictor is developed or evaluated. The robustness theorems also rewrite an analytical upper bound as cost(X,predicted)=cost(X,true)+O(error), which does not follow from the separate big-O bounds.

The empirical results are not credible under the stated metric. With n=1000 and uniform queries, any binary comparison tree requires Omega(log n) comparisons per access, yet Figure 4 reports only about 20,000–35,000 total comparisons for 20,000 accesses. Figure 3 also does not exhibit the severe degeneration predicted for the monotone-priority baseline by Theorem 2.14. In Figure 5, prediction-independent baselines change by large factors as only KL error is purportedly varied, but the protocol does not explain what else changes. Tie handling, zero observed frequencies, error-bar meaning, and distribution construction are unspecified.

Evaluation covers only small synthetic static-BST experiments; there are no dynamic, update, B-tree/external-memory, real-workload, runtime, or memory experiments despite these being major claims. The novelty discussion also does not adequately distinguish the construction from classical weighted/biased randomized search trees and existing entropy-optimal or working-set structures. Together with the proof and experimental inconsistencies, this makes rejection more appropriate despite the promising core BST idea.

The tier-size and ancestor-count argument essentially establishes an O(1+log(1/w_x)) expected-depth guarantee for arbitrary positive weights, improving conceptually on the Zipf-specific baseline.

The counterexamples for using raw frequency priorities motivate the composite design well. Likewise, the cross-entropy/KL interpretation provides an intuitive way to express degradation under inaccurate frequency predictions, once interpreted as an upper-bound comparison rather than an exact cost difference.

The paper ambitiously connects BSTs, external-memory B-trees, dynamic updates, and temporal locality. It is generally organized clearly, and the experimental section includes several classical and learning-augmented baselines, multiple synthetic distributions, imperfect predictions, and repeated trials.

Theorem C.2(3) claims that changing a weight from w to w' touches O(|log_B(w'/w)|) nodes, but its proof merely proposes deletion and reinsertion, which yields O(log_B(1/w)+log_B(1/w')) instead. Because of the floor in the tier definition, an arbitrarily small multiplicative change can cross a tier boundary and cause a nontrivial structural change; resampling the random offset at every update worsens this issue. Theorems D.1, D.2, D.10, and D.11—and hence the advertised dynamic and robustness results—rely directly on this unsupported bound.

The dynamic access model has an unresolved timing/indexing problem. The score w(i) changes at x(i), but a search tree must locate x(i) under the old priority before updating it unless a pointer is supplied. Moreover, work(i,x(i)) is defined using the next occurrence after i, so the claimed depth at time i is based on a future interval, whereas the pre-access tree contains the score from the preceding interval. The paper needs a precise oracle interface, order of search/update operations, and cost accounting; as written, the per-access working-set conclusion does not follow.

The static statements omit an essential additive constant. Since depth counts vertices, every access costs at least one, yet the paper claims O(log(1/p_x)) depth and defines the static optimum as mH(p), both of which can approach zero when one key has probability near one. The valid form is O(1+log(1/p_x)) and total cost O(m+mH(p)). This also makes claims that prediction error causes an exactly additive m·KL overhead stronger than what the proofs establish.

In Corollary C.6, an L-infinity-close q can assign an arbitrarily tiny positive mass to an item having p_x at most epsilon, making p_x log(1/q_x) unbounded; the proof's assertion that such an item has O(log_B n) depth under either p or q is unjustified. Consequently, the derived L2, total-variation, and Hellinger guarantees also do not follow.

strengths: The central idea—grouping weights into doubly logarithmic tiers and randomly breaking ties—is simple and intuitive. It avoids the pathological chains produced by raw frequency priorities and plausibly yields an entropy-sensitive static Treap for arbitrary distributions.
The static BST argument is concise and largely self-contained, while the counterexamples for two alternative priority assignments help motivate the particular construction.

The paper ambitiously connects weighted Treaps to prediction robustness, external-memory B-Trees, and temporal locality, and compares against several learned and classical baselines. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-2iivtu5u/call-39b6382f69744c22a2cdb477c59e2972/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: Several central bounds are false under the paper's own convention that root depth is one. The claimed O(log(1/w_x)) depth tends to zero as w_x tends to one. Likewise, for frequencies (m-1,1), the claimed O(mH(p)) total cost is only O(log m), although processing m accesses costs at least m. The appropriate statements require additive terms, such as O(1+log(1/w_x)) and O(m(1+H(p))); this issue propagates through the BST, B-Tree, and dynamic results.

The dynamic maintenance guarantee is not proved. Corollary 2.7 and Theorem C.2(3) claim an update cost proportional to |log(w'/w)|, but the cited delete-then-insert argument yields a sum of depths, not this difference. Moreover, the dynamic proofs redraw the random offset whenever a score changes, so an arbitrarily small same-tier change can reorder the node within its tier while the claimed bound approaches zero. Theorems D.1, D.10, and the working-set results all depend on this unsupported step.

The robustness arguments misuse upper bounds. From cost(X,e-w)=O(A_e-w) and A_e-w <= A_w+error, one cannot conclude cost(X,e-w)=cost(X,w)+O(error) without proving that A_w is comparable to the actual cost(X,w). No such lower bound is given. Similarly, the static analysis establishes a cross-entropy upper bound, not that the actual overhead is exactly m times the KL divergence.

The stated working-set guarantee is anticipatory rather than the standard working-set property: work(i,x(i)) counts distinct keys until the next access, whereas the standard per-access bound uses keys since the previous access. The timing of prediction, priority update, and access is not specified sufficiently to resolve this. The required B=Omega(log^1.1 n) also excludes B=2, despite repeated claims about dynamic BSTs. Lemma D.8's permutation claim fails for finite sequences when multiple keys never reappear, and Figure 7's caption reverses the proof's inequality.

The B-Tree extension is too sketchy to verify or reproduce. The paper does not establish that gluing independently constructed tier B-Treaps preserves the required B-Tree invariants, nor does it describe the update algorithm supporting the strongest bound. The proof also incorrectly states C_t=O(B^(2^t)) instead of the weaker O(B^(2^(t+1))), and describes constant probability 1-delta as 'with high probability.'

The empirical evidence is not credible as currently reported. It covers only small synthetic static-BST experiments, with no dynamic, B-Tree, update-cost, real-data, runtime, or memory evaluation and no code link. The setup simultaneously says n=1000, varies m, labels the axis 'Number of Accesses,' and calls it the number of unique items. Under the stated uniform experiment with n=1000 and m=20000, any BST needs at least 179,740 comparisons using the paper's depth convention, yet Figure 4 reports roughly 20,000–35,000. Furthermore, with the stated uniform weights, the proposed priorities are simply a constant plus i.i.d. uniform noise and therefore induce exactly the same distribution as a randomized Treap, contrary to the large reported gap.

The related-work discussion does not adequately distinguish the static construction from classical biased or weighted randomized search trees and entropy-optimal alphabetic trees. Consequently, the originality and significance of the sound static core remain insufficiently established.

Its proof silently assumes q_x is at least 1/(1000n), and Corollaries C.7-C.9 inherit this problem.

The paper repeatedly describes KL- or MAE-dependent terms as exact additive overhead over the realized oracle cost, whereas the analysis supplies only upper bounds. The valid static conclusion is an O(m(H(p)+D_KL(p||q))) bound; an additive comparison to the actual cost requires an additional lower-bound argument or more careful wording.

The empirical evidence is limited to synthetic, static BST access counts. There are no dynamic-update or B-tree experiments, real traces, block-I/O or latency measurements, or optimal-static-tree baseline, so the broad practical-performance claims are not yet well supported.

The relation to classical biased or weight-sensitive randomized search trees should be sharper, and numerous notation inconsistencies—such as log bases, time ranges, reversed working-set/interval statements, and the meaning of “with high probability 1-delta”—make the more delicate results harder to verify and reproduce.

strengths: The composite priority -floor(log log(1/w_x)) plus random tie-breaking is simple and insightful. The tier argument gives a plausible expected-depth guarantee for arbitrary weight distributions, substantially broadening the Zipfian-only setting emphasized in prior work. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-03/reviews/icml2025--gpt56_sol/review-experiment-lb5tfb_9/call-0f90dca79f2f4b739bfe87b27fc30ce9/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The adversarial examples help explain why using raw frequencies or coarser logarithmic priorities can produce poor trees.

Extending the construction to external-memory B-Treaps and considering time-varying scores are potentially useful directions. The cross-entropy/KL viewpoint also provides an interpretable connection between prediction error and an upper bound on access cost.
The paper is generally organized around clearly stated objectives, and the experiments include several classical and learning-augmented baselines across multiple synthetic distributions.
weaknesses: The central depth and static-optimality statements omit a necessary additive constant. Since depth counts vertices, it cannot be O(log(1/w_x)) when w_x approaches one. Correspondingly, O(m Ent(p)) is false: for p=(1-1/m,1/m), m Ent(p)=O(log m), while every successful lookup costs at least one comparison and hence total cost is Omega(m). The correct form is O(1+log(1/w_x)) and O(m(1+Ent(p))). This also invalidates the stated OPT formulas and several robustness comparisons as written.

The claimed update bound O(|log(w'/w)|) in Corollary 2.7 and Theorem C.2 is not proved and is generally false. Delete-and-reinsert yields a sum of old and new depths, not their logarithmic ratio. Moreover, an arbitrarily small weight change across a tier boundary can make a node cross Theta(log |S_t|) expected ancestors. The dynamic results in Appendix D explicitly rely on this unsupported bound; a different amortized argument might salvage some total-cost conclusions, but it is not supplied.

The B-Treap extension is too cursory for its claims. Reconnecting independently constructed per-tier B-Treaps is not shown to preserve all B-tree invariants and update guarantees. The proof also infers B=O(C_t^(1/2)) from only an upper bound on C_t, and the simultaneous high-probability claims are asserted without an appropriate case analysis or union bound.

The working-set construction uses future next-access information, so it is not an online working-set guarantee in the usual sense. There is also an indexing ambiguity: the score of the queried key changes at time i, yet the theorem bounds its access depth using that new score without explaining how the node is located before updating it. The relation to the conventional past-looking working-set bound needs a rigorous reindexing and operational description.

Several robustness claims are overstated or false. The KL analysis provides only an asymptotic upper bound O(m(H(p)+D_KL(p||q))), not an exact additive increase of m D_KL. More seriously, the L-infinity, L2, total-variation, and Hellinger corollaries do not follow without clipping or a lower bound on q: a coordinate can have p_x at most epsilon and q_x arbitrarily close to zero, keeping L-infinity error small while making p_x log(1/q_x) arbitrarily large.

The empirical evidence is insufficient and appears internally inconsistent. Only static synthetic lookups are evaluated; there are no dynamic working-set, B-tree I/O, update-cost, real-data, construction-time, or prediction-cost experiments. The axes are described inconsistently, and the plotted scale conflicts with the claimed metric: for uniform access with n=1000 and m=20000, Figures 2-4 report roughly 20000-35000 total comparisons, whereas any BST requires an average of order log n comparisons, implying roughly 200000 comparisons. Figures 5 and 6 also report substantially different costs at zero KL divergence despite nominally sharing n=5000 and m=10000. Thus the experiments cannot presently validate the performance claims or be reproduced from the provided description.

The paper is generally well organized, motivates the problem clearly, and includes synthetic comparisons against several learned and classical search structures.
weaknesses: Several central static bounds are formally false because they omit the unavoidable unit cost per access. With the paper's definition of depth as the number of vertices on the root-to-item path, the correct bound is O(1 + log(1/w_x)), not O(log(1/w_x)). For example, with probabilities (1-1/m, 1/m), the claimed O(m H(p)) total cost is O(log m), whereas any comparison tree costs at least m. Consequently, the stated entropy benchmark, static-optimality formulas, and KL robustness results all require an additive O(m) term.

The claimed weight-update bound O(|log(w'/w)|) in Corollary 2.7 and Theorem C.2 is not proved and does not follow from deleting and reinserting the item, as asserted in the appendix; those operations give bounds depending on log(1/w) + log(1/w'). Moreover, an arbitrarily small weight change across a discretized tier boundary changes the integral priority by one and can require rotations, contradicting a bound tending to zero with |log(w'/w)|. Later dynamic results repeatedly rely on this claim, while also resampling the random offset on every update, which can reorganize a same-tier Treap even for a tiny weight change.

The dynamic working-set analysis has an unresolved timing/model inconsistency. work(i,x(i)) is defined using the next occurrence after the current access, yet the theorem charges the current lookup according to the tree after assigning that score. Updating the priority before lookup requires already locating the node, while updating it afterward only affects the next lookup. A reindexing may recover a related total bound, but the stated per-access theorem and proof do not establish it.

Several additional theoretical claims contain substantive gaps or errors. The L-infinity robustness proof incorrectly lower-bounds q_x using a lower bound on p_x; q_x can be arbitrarily small while satisfying the stated L-infinity condition. The interval sizes in Lemma D.8 are not necessarily a permutation when multiple items never reappear. The high-probability B-Treap guarantees lack a union-bound argument across tiers and updates, and the failure-probability notation reuses the parameter controlling B.

The robustness discussion repeatedly says the additional cost is exactly or linearly equal to KL divergence or prediction MAE, but the analysis supplies only one-sided big-O upper bounds with hidden constants and tier-rounding effects. Figure 6 does not establish linearity through a fit or statistical test and is visibly non-monotone at some points.

The empirical evidence is too limited for the broad performance claims: it uses only small synthetic workloads, gives an underspecified SLSQP procedure for generating prediction errors, and does not evaluate the proposed dynamic method, B-Treap implementation, real learned predictors, update costs, external-memory behavior, wall-clock time, or memory. Reproduction details and code availability are also absent. Given that the static core appears useful but major update, dynamic, and robustness claims are not convincingly established, rejection is currently more appropriate.
